title: CAST Moves the Full TCP/IP Stack into Hardware at 100 Gbps - Semiwiki
gist: CAST has launched TCPIP-100G, a synthesizable IP core that runs a complete TCP/IP stack — connection setup, retransmission, flow and congestion control — entirely in hardware at up to 100 Gbps with no host processor, supporting up to 32,768 sessions configured at synthesis time. The pitch is deterministic latency and freed CPU cores for AI/HPC clusters, SmartNICs and NVMe-over-TCP, but the announcement publishes no area, clock frequency, power or throughput-under-loss figures, and hardware TCP trades software flexibility for efficiency.

themes.theme: Full-stack hardware offload versus partial accelerators

insights.claim: CAST's TCPIP-100G is a synthesizable IP core implementing a complete TCP/IP stack in hardware for ASICs and FPGAs, transmitting and receiving at up to 100 Gbps without depending on a host processor.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A licensable full-stack networking block lets system builders skip a CPU and its software stack entirely — a new competitive axis against merchant NIC silicon.
insights.quote: a synthesizable intellectual-property core that implements a complete TCP/IP stack in hardware for ASICs and FPGAs
insights.locator: Key takeaways — CAST has introduced TCPIP-100G

insights.claim: The core autonomously opens, maintains and closes TCP connections and handles retransmission plus flow and congestion control inside the datapath, which distinguishes it from a checksum engine or a NIC block that accelerates a few operations while leaving connection management to software.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The offload boundary is the whole thing, not the easy parts — the right comparison set is TOE and SmartNIC silicon, not checksum offload features.
insights.quote: this is not simply a checksum engine or a network-interface block that accelerates a few expensive operations while leaving connection management to software
insights.locator: Key takeaways — That distinction is important

insights.claim: The functional scope — base IPv4, ARP with cache, ICMP ping replies, 802.1Q VLAN tagging, checksums and jumbo frames, plus optional DHCP client, out-of-order reassembly and a UDP stack with IGMPv3 multicast — makes the block closer to an autonomous network subsystem than a narrow transport accelerator.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Feature completeness is what makes a CPU-less endpoint viable; incomplete stacks force a host back into the design and destroy the cost argument.
insights.quote: these functions make the block closer to an autonomous network subsystem than a narrow transport accelerator
insights.locator: The base configuration covers IPv4, ARP and an ARP cache

insights.claim: A separate path forwards other IP traffic to the surrounding system, so unsupported protocols do not break the design.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: An escape hatch for protocol coverage gaps reduces integration risk — a practical detail that determines whether the IP actually gets designed in.
insights.locator: Options add a DHCP client, out-of-order TCP-packet reassembly

themes.theme: Synthesis-time configurability as a cost lever

insights.claim: TCPIP-100G can be synthesized to support as many as 32,768 simultaneous TCP sessions and can operate as either client or server.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Session-count ceiling determines which markets it can address — 32k sessions reaches storage and appliance scale but not hyperscale front-end load balancing.
insights.quote: can be synthesized to support as many as 32,768 simultaneous sessions
insights.locator: For an integrating system, the programming model is comparatively simple

insights.claim: Because session count is fixed at synthesis time, designers trade silicon area and memory requirements against connection density instead of paying for unused capacity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Area-scales-with-need economics is the core advantage of IP over fixed merchant silicon in cost-sensitive embedded and edge designs.
insights.quote: designers can trade silicon area and memory requirements against connection density instead of paying for unused capacity
insights.locator: Because the session count is configured at synthesis time

insights.claim: Cut-through mode starts delivering payload before the complete packet is buffered and verified to minimise latency and memory use, while store-and-forward waits for verification and delivers in order, favouring integrity and predictable behaviour.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: An explicit latency-versus-integrity dial lets one IP serve both HFT-style low-latency and storage-integrity workloads — widening the licensable market.
insights.quote: In cut-through mode, the core begins delivering payload before the complete packet has been buffered and verified, minimizing latency and memory use.
insights.locator: CAST also exposes a meaningful architectural choice

insights.claim: Runtime controls over MAC and IP addresses, filters, retransmission policy, TCP window sizes and maximum segment size let a single hardware build serve different workloads without respinning silicon.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Runtime tunability partially offsets the flexibility loss of hardening the stack — the key objection any hardware-TCP buyer raises.
insights.locator: Runtime controls cover MAC and IP addresses, filters, retransmission policy

insights.claim: Integration uses standard AMBA interfaces — a 512-bit AXI4-Stream datapath, a 32-bit AXI4-Lite or optional APB3 control interface, and a 2,048-bit AXI4 connection to external memory — with packet processing and register access on separate clock domains.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A 2,048-bit external memory port is a large integration commitment — it hints the design leans heavily on off-chip memory bandwidth, a hidden system cost.
insights.quote: a 512-bit AXI4-Stream datapath, a 32-bit AXI4-Lite or optional APB3 control interface, and a 2,048-bit AXI4 connection to external memory

insights.claim: The core is intentionally independent of the chosen external-memory technology, memory controller, Ethernet MAC and PHY, though it can be pre-integrated with CAST or third-party MAC IP.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Vendor-agnostic integration lowers the switching cost of adopting the IP and lets CAST attach to whatever MAC/PHY the customer already licenses.
insights.quote: The core is intentionally independent of the chosen external-memory technology, memory controller, Ethernet MAC, and PHY
insights.locator: Packet processing and register access occupy separate clock domains

insights.claim: Deliverables include synthesizable Verilog RTL or a targeted FPGA netlist, a testbench, scripts and documentation, with a UVM verification environment available as an option.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Offering both RTL and FPGA netlist targets both prototype and volume-ASIC customers; UVM as a paid option is a margin upsell typical of IP business models.
insights.locator: Deliverables include synthesizable Verilog RTL or a targeted FPGA netlist

insights.claim: The programming model is deliberately simple: firmware writes network and connection parameters into control registers and then streams application data in and out while the core does all protocol work.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Low software burden shortens time-to-integration, which is usually the real adoption barrier for networking IP rather than raw performance.
insights.locator: For an integrating system, the programming model is comparatively simple

themes.theme: Why hardware TCP matters at 100 Gbps

insights.claim: At 100 Gbps a link carries 12.5 gigabytes per second before protocol overhead, so processing packets, updating thousands of TCP state machines, recovering losses and enforcing congestion windows can consume substantial CPU cycles and introduce scheduling jitter.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Quantifies why software networking breaks down at line rate — the arithmetic behind the whole offload market, including DPU and SmartNIC demand.
insights.quote: At 100 Gbps, the line carries 12.5 gigabytes per second before protocol overhead.

insights.claim: Moving the complete stack into dedicated logic can make latency more deterministic, release processor cores for application work, and reduce data movement and instruction overhead from software networking.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Freed CPU cores translate directly into cost-per-workload savings — the economic argument that decides offload adoption in datacenters.

insights.claim: Network processing is becoming a bottleneck between fast accelerators, storage devices and memory systems in AI and HPC clusters, hyperscale infrastructure, SmartNICs and NVMe-over-TCP storage.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Names the four demand pools for hardware TCP — NVMe-over-TCP in particular is a fast-growing storage protocol that makes offload near-mandatory.
insights.quote: network processing can become a bottleneck between fast accelerators, storage devices, and memory systems
insights.locator: Those benefits are relevant to AI and high-performance-computing clusters

insights.claim: A host-independent stack enables compact endpoints with no general-purpose CPU at all, plus appliances that keep moving traffic even when host software is constrained.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Removing the CPU removes a BOM line and an attack surface — opens edge and appliance designs that were previously uneconomic.
insights.locator: A host-independent stack also enables compact endpoints

themes.theme: Unpublished metrics and the flexibility trade-off

insights.claim: The practical value cannot yet be judged because the announcement publishes no FPGA resource use or ASIC area, clock frequency, external-memory bandwidth, power, achieved throughput across packet sizes, connection churn, or performance under loss and reordering.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: An explicit checklist of the numbers to demand before believing the claim — 100 Gbps at large packet sizes is very different from 100 Gbps under churn and loss.
insights.quote: The practical value will ultimately depend on implementation results that the announcement does not publish
insights.locator: The practical value will ultimately depend on implementation results

insights.claim: Hardware TCP trades software flexibility for efficiency, so standards evolution, security policy and exceptional network conditions all require careful system design around the fixed core.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The structural risk of hardening protocols: a congestion-control or security standard change can strand silicon, which is why software stacks have historically won.
insights.quote: Hardware TCP also trades software flexibility for efficiency, so standards evolution, security policy, and exceptional network conditions require careful system design.
insights.locator: The practical value will ultimately depend on implementation results

insights.claim: The broader significance is that reliable Ethernet networking becomes a configurable hardware building block rather than a software workload attached to the product.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: If networking migrates from software to licensable IP blocks, value shifts toward IP vendors and away from CPU cycles sold to run stacks.
insights.quote: reliable Ethernet networking becomes a configurable hardware building block rather than a software workload attached to the product
insights.locator: Still, TCPIP-100G represents an important option
